The wind howled a mournful tune, rattling the loose corrugated iron sheets of the makeshift structure. Inside, a single flickering candle cast dancing shadows that elongated and distorted, making the small space feel even more confined. A worn blanket served as both door and curtain, doing little to deter the cold that seeped in from every crack. A collection of salvaged items – a cracked mirror, a faded plastic flower, a stack of well-thumbed paperbacks – were carefully arranged, giving the impression of a deliberate, if unconventional, dwelling. Nancy decided to make the porta-potty her home.

Rust-stained and leaning precariously, the wooden fence wound its way through the overgrown garden, a testament to years of neglect. Some sections were missing entirely, creating wide gaps that invited passage, while others were reinforced with hastily tied wire, forming a formidable, if haphazard, barrier. It seemed to have no clear purpose, neither containing the riotous growth within nor repelling the curious gaze of passersby. Perhaps its original intent had been lost to time, or perhaps it had always been a symbol of ambiguity. The fence was confused about whether it was supposed to keep things in or keep things out.

He yearned for the simple gesture, the defiant drag, but the law remained an impenetrable wall. He wondered why at 18 he was old enough to go to war, but not old enough to buy cigarettes.

From his own window, he watched, mesmerized by the destructive beauty, the sheer force of the inferno. Yet, just last week, he'd been denied a pack of cigarettes, the clerk citing state law and his age. The irony was a bitter taste in his mouth, a confusing juxtaposition of expectations and restrictions that left him feeling adrift in a sea of adult contradictions. He wondered why at 18 he was old enough to go to war, but not old enough to buy cigarettes.
